extracted.intended_audience: Applicants for NIH Individual NRSAs (F30/F31) — predoctoral fellowship candidates and their mentors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for F30/F31 NRSA applicants on when and how to contact NIH program officers (before submission, after review/summary statement, and before resubmission), including what to ask, how to compose communications, and procedural tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact program officers before submission and after review
rubrics_metrics.description: Contacting program officers before the first submission and after review of virtually all grant applications, including F30 and F31 applications, is highly recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Program officers can advise about institute enthusiasm, priorities, study section trends, and detailed requirements (e.g., animal/human subjects). Procedure: Do not wait until a week or two before the deadline; contact when you have a reasonable draft of your specific aims. Identify the officer via the FOA (Section VII, Agency Contacts). You may contact officers at two or more institutes at this preliminary stage if programmatically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the correct program officer via the FOA
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify your program officer by searching the FOA ('F30 FOA' or 'F31 FOA') and following the link in Section VII (Agency Contacts) to program officer contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check Key Dates to avoid expired announcements. Use the FOA's Agency Contacts links rather than guessing or relying on third-party listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact early — when you have a reasonable draft of specific aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not wait until a week or two before your proposal is due to contact a program officer; the time to contact is when you have a reasonable draft of your specific aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if aims change, early contact allows meaningful guidance. Contacting too late reduces usefulness and may be impractical for the officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose a concise email with central question, hypothesis, and attached specific aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose an email starting with a (very) few sentences highlighting your central question and the hypothesis you are proposing to test, and attach your specific aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move quickly to clear, brief questions (most important: institute's potential enthusiasm). Indicate in the brief intro that specific aims are attached so the officer has immediate context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase questions clearly and prioritize asking about institute enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Move quickly to the questions you have, phrased as clearly and briefly as possible; your most important question will be about the institute’s potential enthusiasm for your proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other questions can ask what to emphasize relative to study section trends, technical aspects, or detailed requirements. Keep questions short and focused to facilitate a helpful response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest phone follow-up for complicated or nuanced issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a complicated question, or if there exist nuances that are difficult to get across in writing, suggest a follow-up by phone in your email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phone conversations are often more productive for back-and-forth and complex topics (especially after receiving the summary statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask your mentor to review the email before sending
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask your mentor to review the email before you send it, as they have considerable experience communicating with program officers and can make valuable suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentor involvement can improve clarity and appropriateness of questions and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow one week for response and send a gentle reminder if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a program officer a week to respond, then e-mail a gentle reminder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A delayed response does not mean disinterest—officers are busy and vary in responsiveness. If you encounter difficulties engaging an officer, your advisor can assist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask, after review, 'how close is the proposal to being funded?'
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive the summary statement, directly ask the program officer: 'how close is the proposal to being funded?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question helps determine whether further action (resubmission, programmatic advocacy) is warranted and guides priorities for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use program officer discussion to understand programmatic priorities and funding likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposal is on the cusp of funding, discuss institute programmatic priorities to determine how strongly your proposal coincides with them; this may help move the proposal up or suggest how to fit priorities for resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic context (funding outlook, priorities) can materially affect funding decisions beyond the summary statement score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss factual errors in reviews but not reviewers' opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviews contain factual errors, discuss these with the program officer in terms of whether they impacted scoring and what to do on resubmission; it is not appropriate to discuss reviewers’ opinions (as opposed to factual errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on correcting objective inaccuracies and clarifying misunderstandings; avoid arguing reviewers' subjective judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use program officer's study-section insight to prioritize resubmission changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers often attended the study section and can provide notes of the discussion; they can help you focus on the most salient issues for resubmission and clarify ambiguous or contradictory reviewer points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the officer did not attend, they have experience reading reviews and can advise how to treat conflicting statements between reviewers or ambiguous points.

rubrics_metrics.name: When you receive the summary statement, prepare (with mentor), list issues, and take notes during calls
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive the summary statement, go through it carefully with your advisor; allow emotions to settle; make a list of major and minor issues; set up a phone conversation with the program officer and take notes during the call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the rationale points with your mentor beforehand. Don't let emotions rule—treat the interaction as professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before resubmission, confirm institute enthusiasm and notify officer of responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Before resubmitting, check that the institute’s potential enthusiasm remains high, funding outlook hasn't changed drastically, and priorities remain the same; let the program officer know that your resubmission is responsive to reviewers’ comments and to the officer’s comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedure mirrors initial contact: brief email with aims/changes and clear questions; this signals responsiveness and maintains the working relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek program officer input on current study section trends and technical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers can provide insight on what aspects of proposals or research areas are drawing special attention in study sections (recent examples include 'rigor' and statistics) and can advise on detailed requirements such as animal or human subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate officer suggestions on emphasis or handling of trending requirements into your application to strengthen review-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for variable officer engagement and involve your advisor if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some program officers are more difficult to engage than others; a delayed or limited response may reflect workload, not disinterest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you encounter difficulty, ask your advisor to help make contact or follow up.
